body:
Rather than start a new project with new tooling, this PR took out the necessary files from the Pantheon repo (https://github.com/ConsenSys/pantheon) so that tooling would be the same across both projects, allowing for easy integration down the line.

Included in this PR are:
- Gradle setup
- Dockerfile
- Spotless
- Error-prone (https://github.com/google/error-prone)
- Int, Hash, Address Types
- RLP encoding
- All other files are required for a successful build (due to imports, etc).

title: Remove web3j submodule - opt for use as dependency instead.
body:
When trying to work with the web3j submodule we ran into some difficulty with imports. Upon reading more on submodules, I found this snippet (source: https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Tools-Submodules):

> It’s quite likely that if you’re using submodules, you’re doing so because you really want to work on the code in the submodule at the same time as you’re working on the code in the main project (or across several submodules). Otherwise you would probably instead be using a simpler dependency management system (such as Maven or Rubygems).

We weren't able to resolve the issue with importing using submodules; considering the above, it is worth reverting back to using web3j as a dependency rather than a submodule because it 1) solves our import issue and 2) is not currently necessary to keep up-to-date with frequent repo changes. Initially it seemed to make sense to use a submodule, but since we're only using it for types at the moment, using a submodule is unnecessary.

body:
## PR Description
This PR adds [google-java-format](https://github.com/google/google-java-format) to the spotlessCheck/spotlessApply step of the gradle build process. 

- The first commit is the only change that was made manually (/build.gradle). 
- The second commit were changes made automatically as part of the spotlessApply step.

Because this is a general code format change which takes place in nearly every file, so it's likely when you go to merge that there will be conflicts. I believe the best course of action will be to do a `git fetch upstream` then `git rebase -Xtheirs upstream/master --autostash` followed by running `./gradlew spotlessApply` on your individual changes. 

## Fixed Issue(s)
Fixes #163

Added the helper functions defined in the spec:
```
First, we define some additional helpers:

Let base_reward_quotient = integer_squareroot(previous_total_balance) // BASE_REWARD_QUOTIENT.
Let base_reward(state, index) = get_effective_balance(state, index) // base_reward_quotient // 5 for any validator with the given index.
Let inactivity_penalty(state, index, epochs_since_finality) = base_reward(state, index) + get_effective_balance(state, index) * epochs_since_finality // INACTIVITY_PENALTY_QUOTIENT // 2 for any validator with the given index.
```

title: BLS reference tests
body:
## PR Description
I've filled out the reference test framework for the official BLS tests from https://github.com/ethereum/eth2.0-tests/

Unfortunately, there are many issues with the input data, so this is a mess. Specific issue are as follows:

```
 * The point compression used is broken. See https://github.com/ethereum/eth2.0-tests/issues/20
 * This leads to extensive and tedious work-arounds in the below. Test 06 is too hard to fix
 * Specifically:
 *   > The c flag is missing
 *   > The a flag is inverted and is at the wrong bit position
 *   > The compressed coordinate ordering is inverted: should be [Im, Re], but is [Re, Im]
 *   > The a flag doesn't always match the Y-coordinate, which matters when interpreting
 *     compressed input data, such as for the aggregation tests.
 * Also
 *   > Our yaml ingester doesn't like the test case 07 input data format (a missing "-")
 * Finally, note that the spec and test data will likely be changing.
```

See [here](https://github.com/ethereum/eth2.0-specs/issues/508) and [here](https://github.com/ethereum/trinity/issues/233) for more on the Y co-ord selection issue.

I've worked around these where I can, but it's not complete. However, I don't believe it's worth spending any more time on this until (a) the spec has stabilised and (b) the test vectors are updated.

Meanwhile, I'm satisfied that our implementation is basically correct. 🙌
author: benjaminion

- during each slot we do this:
  should we process this block?
  - if yes: 
    - run through all blockless state transitions from parentBlock.slot to block.slot -1
    - do state transition for block.slot
    - run through all blockless state transitions from block.slot to latest slot
  - if no:
    - run through blockless state transition for latest slot

<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/artemis/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
Fixing an off by one error in shuffle that I created.  

in shuffle(), a list of integers was originally created this way:

```java
int[] indices = new int[listSize];
for (int i = 0; i < listSize; i++) {
  indices[i] = i;
}
```

I changed it to this for performance reasons:

```java
int[] indices = IntStream.rangeClosed(0, listSize).toArray();
```

Then realized that I made the list too big and now I am correcting it like this:

```java
int[] indices = IntStream.rangeClosed(0, listSize-1).toArray();
```

🤦‍♂️

title: Upgrade SSZ to v0.5.1
body:
## PR Description
This change implements v0.5.1 compliant hash_tree_root and related helper functions, and refactors our codebase to use the new hash_tree_root logic. This probably isn't the most clean way to do it, but that can come at a later time.

### SSZ Background
**Basic Types**
 - `bool`
 - `uintN`: `N`-bit unsigned integer (where `N` is in `[8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]`)
 - `byte`: This is just an alias for `uint8`, already defined above as a base type.

**Collections**
 - `tuple`: ordered fixed-length homogeneous collection of values
   - angle bracket notation `[type, N]`, e.g. `["uint64", N]`
 - `list`: ordered variable-length homogenous collection of values
   - angle bracket notation `[type]`, e.g. `["uint64"]`

**Other Composite Types**
 - `container`: ordered heterogenous collection of values.
   - key-pair curly bracket notation `{}`, e.g. `{'foo': "uint64", 'bar': "bool"}`

### Implications for Us
Given the above definitions, we can deduce a couple of things about our typing:
 - `Bytes` is (in general) a list of basic types, as it holds an arbitrary number of `byte`s.
 - `Bytes32`, `Bytes48`, etc. are tuples of basic types, as they hold a fixed-number of `byte`s.
 - All of our custom types are SSZ containers (of containers of ...) until they are defined individually by either a basic SSZ type or a collection of SSZ types.

Each of the above types defined above in **SSZ Background** have different rules about how they must be serialized and how their hash tree root is calculated, so it is no longer sufficient to simply call `SSZ.hash_tree_root(type.toBytes())`, because `Bytes` no longer accurately describes the type's SSZ context...it just holds bytes.

### The Change
I'm still working out the best way to split these changes up into a library (Tuweni) part and an implementation (Artemis) part, but for the moment all hash tree root logic lives in Artemis. 

 - Remove the general `hash_tree_root(Bytes)` function and any convenience functions which wrap it.
 - Define a specific `hash_tree_root_basic_type(Bytes)` function which correctly calculates the hash tree root of a basic SSZ object and of a tuple of basic SSZ objects (for types such as long, UnsignedLong, or Bytes32 object).
 - Define a specific `hash_tree_root_list_of_basic_types(List<? extends Bytes>)` function which correctly calculates the hash tree root of a list of basic SSZ objects (for types such a Bytes object, or a List<? extends Bytes>, etc.).

## See Also
 - https://github.com/ethereum/eth2.0-specs/blob/v0.5.1/specs/simple-serialize.md
 - https://github.com/ethereum/eth2.0-specs/blob/v0.5.1/utils/phase0/minimal_ssz.py

title: Fixes get_crosslink_committees_at_slot() logic and test
body:
## PR Description
Fixes get_crosslink_committees_at_slot() logic and penalizeValidatorDecrementsBadActorAndIncrementsWhistleblower test with accurate mock data.

penalizeValidatorDecrementsBadActorAndIncrementsWhistleblower originally initiated the validator list at size 3. The number of validators required to remove this error is supposed to be at least 64, since split splits the validator list into 64 committees. The issue was that split would return empty lists for the empty committees - and the divide by zero error was due to the first item in the shuffling list in get_crosslink_committees_at_slot being an empty list. Thus, testing with 64 validators should fix the problem, since each committee will be non-empty.

title: Dynamic output fields
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/artemis/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
**Changes and workflow**
1. Output Fields for events are added in config.toml file under [output.fields] section with a getter inside ArtemisConfiguration. 
2. These fields are added to a lookup map called "eventOutputFields" inside EventHandler.class by fetching from ArtemisConfiguration.
3. When event is triggered, this map "eventOutputFields" is looked up for fields to output and "filterOutputFields" method is called on triggered event Object.
4. This method will compute the fields and it's values to output and stores it in the state called "outputFieldMap" inside event Object.
5. Based on providerType[JSON, CSV], respective methods toJson() or toCSV() is called. These methods will refer to  "outputFieldMap" to generate the respective output Type.



## Fixed Issue(s)
<!-- Please link to fixed issue(s) here using format: fixes #<issue number> -->
<!-- Example: "fixes #2" -->

Adds further checking for created G1 and G2 points to ensure that they do indeed lie in the correct subgroups. We do this by multiplying by the group order and checking that we get the identity point. This is relevant to points deserialised from hex and for randomly created points.

Failing to do this could result in verifying signatures that other clients consider invalid, for example.

Updates tests accordingly.
author: benjaminion

title: Introduce metrics abstraction
body:
## PR Description
Introduces the abstraction layer for metrics capture from Pantheon.

A `MetricsSystem` instance is created and added to the `ServiceConfig` object so each service can create counters/gauges/etc as needed which are then reported through the Prometheus endpoint provided by the `MetricsServer` service.

Note that in a micro service future, each micro service would run its own `MetricsServer` service and have an independent `MetricsSystem` instance but we only want a single prometheus endpoint per JVM instance.

I'm not 100% sure `MetricsService` should be an actual service but it needs to tie into life-cycle so it seems to fit.

## Related Issue(s)
#712

title: Implementation of new (draft) hash-to-G2
body:
## PR Description
This is a Java implementation of the new IETF (draft) standard hash-to-curve method for Ethereum 2.0. The underlying library is Milagro AMCL 1.4, though there is lots that I ended up adding to this.

References:
 * The draft standard: https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-irtf-cfrg-hash-to-curve-05
 * Reference implementations: https://github.com/algorand/bls_sigs_ref
 * Interesting background: https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/403.pdf
 
This code is based on the reference implementations in Python and C, and test vectors are taken from there. My implementation is not constant-time, but that should not be a problem for Eth2 use cases (all hashed messages are public information).

## Status

A complete implementation of the new hash-to-curve standard as of 31/12/2019

## Performance

(Based on an outdated version)

On my Linux VM
  - The Python reference code ~ 200ms per hash
  - The C reference code ~ 1.0ms per hash (doesn't include the transformation to affine representation, and shortcuts the initial SHA256)
  - This code ~ 2.9ms per hash

Here's a [flame graph](https://benjaminion.xyz/hashToCurve_20191024.svg) (it's interactive - click on the bars to zoom in). I'm struggling to see much room for further improvement.

## TODO

Nothing more here. Note that a wider BLS refactor is underway: #1080
author: benjaminion

title: Guava `EventBus` exception handling fix (#850)
body:
## PR Description

The rationale behind this fix proposal is the following:

* Guava's `EventBus` and exceptions in handlers can't really be "bubbled up" because they are thrown in an executor thread and so they should always be somehow handled; I guess that's why `EventBus` doesn't even let custom exception handlers re-throw them (the second answer in that SO thread highlights this behavior).
* On the other hand: is it true in general (or at least commonly) that the correct behavior for an Artemis handler, when it encounters a spec violation, is just to abort and log an error (without stack trace)?
* Assuming that the answer is yes, something like the exception handler proposed here could make sense (possibly with some integrations to `isSpecFailure`).
* If that's not the case though, each and every handler should specifically handle assert failures locally.

## Fixed Issue(s)

Fixes #850
author: circlespainter

title: Start from disk
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/artemis/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
This PR adds functionality to start Artemis using the content on disk. If the startFromDisk boolean is set to true in config.toml, it loads the contents of Store from disk and sets the current node slot according to the genesis time of the last finalized beacon state on disk. Also, it only loads the BeaconBlocks and BeaconStates into memory that is necessary, meaning the ones that will be used by the fork choice methods, to not overflow the memory. 

Artemis validators start producing blocks immediately, start attesting at the start of the next epoch (due to attestation duties being assigned at the start of epochs) and Artemis is able to justify and finalize in about to 2 epochs, similar to a regular start.

title: Update deposit contract to v0.9.0
body:
## PR Description
Updates the deposit contract to v0.9.
This requires adding the `DepositData.hash_tree_root` as an additional argument that is checked. Our `hash_tree_root` implementation is correct as it matches the ssz reference tests, but the check failed for inputs that Artemis considered valid.  This is because Artemis reverses the byte arrays it passes into the deposit contract, so the data the deposit contract worked with was backwards. Artemis then reversed the data coming from the deposit events so it saw the data as valid again.

This removes both reversals so the data is valid inside the deposit contract and Artemis is compatible with other clients in how it processes the deposit events.

Also updates ganache-cli to the latest stable release so it can be installed on macOS Catalina (node-gyp failed to compile on the version we were using).

`GanacheController` was modified to use a temporary file so it works even if `pow/src/main/resources` hasn't been created (there's no tracked files in it so git won't create it automatically).

title: Implement BeaconBlocksByRoot request
body:
## PR Description
Adds support for the beacon blocks by root req/resp method. This requires supporting responses which return a stream of responses. So we now have three cases - no response (GOODBYE), single response (STATUS) and stream of responses (BLOCKS_BY_ROOT).

There's some ugliness under the covers to make no-response and single-response requests work nicely while still supporting the streaming of responses where the could be multiple and not have to collect all the responses into a list.  The `Peer` class provides a nice simple API for external callers to use which handles nearly all those details.

The API for multiple-response handling may need to be tweaked further in the future - the tests work best when it is collected into a List - will have to see how it works when in actual use. The main oddity there is that the data is sent to a callback handler but the "response complete" and error signals are sent via the returned `CompletableFuture`. We may want to pass them through to the callback handler instead but the tests work out nicer with the current approach, so let's see how it goes...

title: Disconnect req/resp streams after the maximum allowed number of responses are received
body:
## PR Description
For req/resp requests like `STATUS` where a single response chunk is expected, the requester is responsible for closing the stream once it's received and the responder does not.

For requests that can have multiple responses, while the responder will close the stream after sending all response chunks, we have a known upper bound on the number of responses we expect (typically the number of blocks we requested) and should enforce that as a limit to avoid processing a never ending stream of responses from the remote peer.

title: [BC-27] Handle propagating blocks
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/artemis/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
Add `BlockPropagationManager` for handling gossiped blocks propagating on the network.  Gossiped blocks are imported if possible, otherwise blocks with unknown parents are added to the `PendingBlocks` set and blocks from a future slot are added to a `FutureBlocks` set.  The `BlockPropagationManager` listens for slot and import events so that it can import pending and future blocks when possible.  The fetching unknown blocks' ancestors will be addressed in a follow-up PR.

As part of this work, some of the events have been reworked and some other ancillary changes have been included:
* Raw block events have been replaced with `BlockProposedEvent` and `GossipedBlockEvent`.
  * This allows the `BlockGossipManager` to more selectively process proposed blocks, and avoid reprocessing gossiped blocks.
* `ProcessedBlockEvent` has been replaced with the more generic `BlockImportedEvent`
* `StateProcessor` now only processes proposed blocks, the processing of gossiped blocks has moved into `BlockPropagationManager`. 
* All block imports now go through the `BlockImporter` class.
* Fork choice logic has been updated to check for future blocks based on `Store` time.
* A `Service` class has been added for structuring basic service lifecycle methods

title: Remodel SyncManager as a continuously running service
body:
## PR Description
Changes `SyncManager` into a service which is expected to continue keeping us in sync as long as it's running, rather than a one-off event to bring us up to sync.  It's actual behaviour is mostly unchanged - it does an initial sync and triggers a new sync whenever a new peer connects.  The two key differences are:
* Exceptions thrown during a sync are logged instead of silently lost because we didn't handle the returned `CompletableFuture`
* If a peer connects while an existing sync is in progress, we schedule a new sync for when that one completes. This ensures that if the peer has a better chain we will eventually get there.

Net result is that we keep running syncs until there is no longer a peer with a better finalised epoch.

`PeerSync` got a bit of reworking so that `SyncManager` could be tested independently of it.  It now accepts the peer to sync to as an argument to the `sync` method rather than the constructor so it can be re-used for multiple syncs.

title: Enable FutureReturnValueIgnored errorprone check
body:
## PR Description
Enables the `FutureReturnValueIgnored` errorprone check and ensures that results of all futures are handled in some way.

Mostly this is done via the introduction of `GoodFuture` (better names welcome) which extends `CompletableFuture` and adds useful methods to make it easier to end the future chain without failing the `FutureReturnValueIgnored` check.  For example `reportExceptions()` which outputs a log if the future is completed exceptionally (like the exception would have been printed by the thread uncaught exception handler).

There's also a few variants of `finish` which can accept and process a value without returning a new future and exceptions are automatically logged. `finish` also makes it easier to handle both success and failure conditions without having to do the `null` checks required by `handle` or `whenComplete`.

title: When syncing, request slots after our latest finalized slot
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/artemis/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
Fix a few issues with `PeerSync`:
* Only request non-finalized slots (slots after the start of our latest finalized epoch).  If we request blocks at our finalized slot, the first block may fail to import, causing us to abort the sync prematurely.  
* Account for the fact that some slots may be empty.  Previously we assumed that blocks would be consecutive - we incremented our startSlot by the requestSize each time.  We now track the most recently returned block's slot and base our next query on this value.
* Sync based on a single `PeerStatus` instance so that we know the blocks we request should be consistent and we can penalize peers if they are not.  
* Complete the peer sync early if the last response was empty
* Add some extra checks to make sure we're only querying when we need to (return early if we're caught up to our peer).

title: Support delaying attestation processing
body:
## PR Description
Introduces a new `AttestationManager` which is roughly equivalent to the `BlockPropagationManager` but for attestations.  It can queue attestations that we're not yet ready to process until later - either based on the slot they are due to be processed in or blocks they depend on.

`PendingBlocks` and `FutureBlocks` have been adapted so they can be reused with attestations.

body:

## PR Description
When a block is gossiped and we don't have the pre-state associated with this block, don't re-gossip the block but do post an event so that `BlockPropagationManager` can track the block. title: Group deposits together by block
body:
## PR Description
Ensures that all deposits in a single block and processed together when creating the genesis state as required by the spec.

Normally we publish a block when we start receiving deposits from the next block, but to ensure the last deposit on the chain is published we also consider a block complete if 5 seconds passes without receiving a deposit.  This isn't ideal as it's possible something just caused a delay in sending new deposits but keeps things running for now.  We will need to follow up to request all deposits from the block that timed out (https://pegasys1.atlassian.net/browse/BC-248) to solve this.

Builds on #1119

title: Remerkable
body:
##  PR Description

This is the implementation of 'backing binary Merkle tree' ('remerkable') concept developed by Protolambda: https://github.com/protolambda/eth-merkle-trees/blob/master/typing_partials.md

#### Benefits: 
- Incremental hashing
- Incremental storage: storing (in memory or on disk) several `BeaconState` modifications from different slots/forks at minimal cost
- Addressing any component of `BeaconState` with a uniform generalized index and generating Merkle proof for it. This might potentially be a part of a state syncing protocol

#### Drawbacks:
- Naive approach slows down large structures iteration (like `validators`). Need some more advanced approach
- Naive approach slows down structure modification. Need to add some write cache and the 'batch' tree update function to avoid the full tree rebuilding on each single modification
- More complicated data structures to manage 

#### Deviations from original concept
- Simplification: no tree `expand`. All structures has 'static' backing tree depth
- `List`s are represented as `Container(Vector, int size)` structures

#### Benchmarks
While block import speed increases significantly due to incremental `hash_tree_root` (BLS verify takes ~85% of time now), pure epoch transition becomes slower `50ms => 370ms` due to slow backing tree validators iteration. The naive backing tree implementation is subject to be optimized in the next optimization round

Avoids port conflicts when running multiple instances on the same host

There is still an interface in place so remote validator signing services could be used later, but there's no point in using GRPC and network sockets while we're hard coded to use the signing service in the same process anyway.

title: Ensure Eth1DataCache and ValidatorCoordinator process slots in sync
body:
The order that slot events were delivered to Eth1DataCache and ValidatorCoordinator was not guaranteed which may result in ValidatorCoordinator producing blocks with incorrect ETH1 data or Eth1DataCache not having the information ValidatorCoordinator needed.

It also led to intermittency in `ValidatorCoordinatorTest` when `Eth1DataCache` had not received a `SlotEvent` and initialised its `currentVotingPeriodStartTime` before `ValidatorCoordinator` asked it for an ETH1 data vote, resulting in `java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: inconsistent range` from the sorted map when retrieving votes.

`ValidatorCoordinator` now directly passes slot events to Eth1DataCache to ensure it has processed the slot event prior to starting to create blocks.

title: Throttle the rate of requests made to the ETH1 node
body:
With the need to retrieve block information for both deposits and building the Eth1 data cache, we're sending a *lot* of requests to the ETH1 node which may overload it and result in timeouts.

This introduces a throttling to limit the number of in-flight requests we have at any point in time.

title: [BC-267] Fix finalized block lookup
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/artemis/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
Currently our storage layer only exposes an API that allows us to query for finalized blocks proposed at a specific slot - if that slot is skipped, an empty value is returned.  This PR adds a new API that allows us to query for the latest finalized block at a slot (the effective block at this slot).  If the slot is skipped, the most recent finalized block is returned.  

`CombinedChainDataClient` and `PeerChainValidator` have been updated to use this new API.

title: [BC-268] Only prune hot blocks prior to latest finalized block
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/artemis/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
Currently, we're pruning our [hotStatesByRoot](https://github.com/PegaSysEng/artemis/blob/cb5d35e69b4577eb3d3904ffdbbab23a20a33e19/storage/src/main/java/tech/pegasys/artemis/storage/MapDbDatabase.java#L60) collection using the epoch boundary of the latest finalized block.  If the epoch boundary is a skipped slot (the finalized block for this epoch is from a slot prior to the epoch boundary slot), this means that we'll end up pruning the finalized state.  Upon restarting the client, we'll hydrate our Store from the database and end up with no finalized state corresponding to our finalized block.  This prevents us from importing new blocks on top of our latest finalized block.

In this PR, the hot block pruning logic has been updated to only prune blocks that are prior to the slot of the latest finalized block.

title: [BC-90] Process rpc responses asynchronously
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/artemis/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
Create new `AsyncResponseProcessor` class for processing responses to outgoing rpc requests asynchronously.  This fixes a few issues:
* [Previously](https://github.com/PegaSysEng/artemis/pull/1182), our response processing time would be considered when evaluating rpc timeouts.  Now, timeouts should only fire if bytes are slow to arrive from the network.
* Previously, if we were slow in processing rpc responses, bytes received from our peer would end up buffered in memory at the libp2p layer.  When an error was encountered, we could close our rpc stream, but those messages buffered in memory would continue to arrive and be processed.  This caused some confusing behavior where messages continued to be processed when a request was considered finished.

Shuffling indexes per epoch in a single list pass is much faster than computing their permutations individually.

```
TransitionBenchmark.Epoch.importBlock              16384    ss   10  0,897 ± 0,042   s/op
TransitionBenchmark.Epoch.importBlock              32768    ss   10  1,638 ± 0,018   s/op
```

## PR Description
`ConnectionManager` now maintains a target range for number of peers to be connected to.  New peers are only connected when the current peer count is below the target range, with enough connection attempts made to reach the top of that range, expecting that some will fail to connect.

title: Support returning async responses from event channels
body:
## PR Description
Adds support to `EventChannel` for methods which return a `SafeFuture`. The method is still asynchronously invoked and the response provided via the future. This will make it easier to move the storage server interfaces over to use `EventChannel` instead of `EventBus` and hide the complexity of managing async results.  Ultimately `AsyncEventTracker` will become unnecessary.

When channels can return a result, only a single subscriber is allowed. Future enhancements could allow for multiple subscribers with various load-balancing or fail-over semantics but we don't need that for now.
author: ajsutton

title: Do not drop static peers when connection limit is reached
body:
## PR Description
Ensure `ConnectionManager` does not disconnect static peers when the peer connection limit is reached.

As a result:
 * Static peers still count towards the connection limit
 * If the connection limit is reached, discovery peers will be disconnected and static ones preserved
 * If the static peers exceed the connection limit by themselves, they will all remain connected but all discovery peers will be disconnected.

This differs from Besu where static peers are not included in the peer limit at all, but should simplify things. You can set the connection limit based on the capacity for number of peers that can be serviced, and independently manage the list of peers you always want to be connected to. With Besu, you have to adjust the peer limit each time you adjust the static peers to maintain the same resource usage.

title: [BC-298] Rework ChainStorageClient initialization
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/artemis/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
Update `ChainStorageClient` to handle its own initialization.  Previously `BeaconChainController` would listen for a `Store` to be posted from the `ChainStorageServer`, which it would then use to initialize the `ChainStorageClient`:
* `BeaconChainController` now receives a `SafeFuture<ChainStorageClient>` that completes once the client is initialized from storage.  `BeaconChainController` currently blocks waiting for the client to initialize.  
    * This necessitates that the `ChainStorageService` be set up first so that any `ChainStorageClient`'s that are created can be initialized.  This will be reworked in [a follow up PR](https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/pull/1268) to clean up service startup logic.

Removing `BeaconChainController` from the initialization process means that the `ChainStorageClient` may be initialized without setting the "best block", as a result `getBestBlockRoot()` and `getBestBlockState()` now return `Optional`'s.  This has resulted in a few additional changes:
* We have a new `ChainStorageClient.subscribeBestBlockInitialized` method for subscribers who need to run logic once the best block is initialized
* The `ArtemisNode` acceptance test utility has been updated to account for the fact that we now need to wait for the head block to be set

Additional fixes include:
* Handling starting up from disk when the database is empty
* Ensuring the `ChainStorageClient.Store` is only ever set once

title: Programmatic logging
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/artemis/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
Updating the logging configuration to support `Log4j2` hot replace of `xml` configuration file, in addition to options in the Teku confg.

The concept applied was to split the logging through Teku into three types:
1) Class logging (the default approach `LogManager.getLogger()`)
2) EventLogger contextual log messages (events occurring with a cadence e.g. SlotEvents)
3) StatusLogger context log messages (events occurring without a cadence e.g. unexpected failures)

The loggers were changed from being defined in default `log4j2.xml` to being programmatically defined. This allows greater flexibility in setup.
Now there are three logging `DESTINATION`s available:
- `CONSOLE` all log messages go to the stdout (no log file is created or written to).
- `FILE` all log messages go to the log file (no output to stdout)
- `BOTH` messages from `EventLogger` and `StatusLogger` are displayed in both the console and file, but class log message only appear in the file.
(NB there is a semaphore to disable output from the `StatusLogger`)
 
Semaphore added for whether color is to be used in output, if color is enabled and the message is output to the log, then the color character is included.

When the storage service fails to start, the beacon chain controller startup hangs waiting for a response from storage.  Since we were using `allOf` to wait for both startups to complete, we never reported the startup failure from the storage service (because we were still waiting for the beacon chain controller to finish starting up).

Added a `allOfFailFast` to `SafeFuture` which, when everything completes successfully is the same as `allOf` but will fail immediately when any of the futures fails. This ensures the failure is reported, even if other services are unable to complete startup until the failed service is available.

title: Optimize backing views
body:
## PR Description

This is the follow up to https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/pull/1133 which had a naive backing tree views implementations with pretty straightforward read/write code (i.e. traverse the whole tree path on every read and modify the whole tree path on every write) which resulted in 4x epoch processing time increase comparing to POJO `BeaconState` implementation. 

This PR optimizes backing views:
- read-only views cache their child views so the composite view traverse performance is somewhat near array traverse 
- a mutable view has backing immutable view plus changes accumulated in a simple `HashMap` (no backing tree modifications are done prior to `commitChanges`) 
- When doing `commitChanges` the changes accumulated in a mutable view are merged with backing immutable view cache to form the created immutable view cache in place. Also the backing binary tree is built in batched manner. This way the view objects which are not changed need not be recreated across any number of transitions. 

The `Validator` container was made immutable for performance reasons: the changes to `Validator` is pretty rare comparing to reads. 

Deprecate `BeaconState.createWritableCopy()` in favor of `BeaconState.updated(Consumer<MutableBeaconState>)` to restrict the scope of using `MutableBeaconState` instances and enforce immutable instances usage.

Piggy tailing a couple of bonus optimizations to this PR which won another ~20% of performance: 
- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/pull/1465/commits/12d666e397980ba560bc698328e8282dd1e59946
- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/pull/1465/commits/6c49148318bdbbd357d399f00d02351e27cc0727
- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/pull/1465/commits/91830d432b67ae041a214dd22e4ac485f32068de

## Benchmarks: 

The preliminary result is that epoch transition speed up is ~4x and is almost the same as original POJO `BeaconState` implementation. 

#### Before:
```
Benchmark                              (validatorsCount)  Mode  Cnt  Score   Error  Units
TransitionBenchmark.Block.importBlock              16384    ss   50  0,266 ± 0,005   s/op
TransitionBenchmark.Block.importBlock              32768    ss   50  0,387 ± 0,004   s/op
TransitionBenchmark.Epoch.importBlock              16384    ss   10  0,897 ± 0,042   s/op
TransitionBenchmark.Epoch.importBlock              32768    ss   10  1,638 ± 0,018   s/op
```
#### After:
```
Benchmark                              (validatorsCount)  Mode  Cnt  Score   Error  Units
TransitionBenchmark.Block.importBlock              16384    ss  250  0,152 ± 0,004   s/op
TransitionBenchmark.Block.importBlock              32768    ss  250  0,183 ± 0,003   s/op
TransitionBenchmark.Epoch.importBlock              16384    ss  100  0,322 ± 0,005   s/op
TransitionBenchmark.Epoch.importBlock              32768    ss  100  0,559 ± 0,020   s/op
```

#### After (with bonus optimizations):
```
Benchmark                              (validatorsCount)  Mode  Cnt  Score   Error  Units
```

title: Introduce Signer as a richer API for signing domain objects
body:
## PR Description
The `MessageSignerService` interface works purely on the signing root value leaving the caller to calculate the signing root for the specific object.  To avoid duplicating that logic and provide a richer domain-object based API for signing, introduce the `Signer` object which takes a domain object, calculates the signing root then uses the `MessageSignerService` to sign it.

Loading of validators is also adjusted to move it in the direction required for loading into the validator client service which won't know the validator index.

title: Use BitSet as backing for Bitlist rather than byte[]
body:
## PR Description
The `Bitlist` implementation was allocating a `byte[]` as backing data, storing one byte per bit in the bitlist.  Instead, use a `BitSet` as backing which combines bits into `long` values reducing the memory required.

The `BitSet` backing version is also faster than the `byte[]` version. The benchmarks are definitely not polished and the error margin is high but they are providing quite stable results on multiple runs.

```
Old implementation:
Benchmark                                        Mode  Cnt         Score        Error  Units
SSZTypes.BitlistBenchmark.countSetBits          thrpt   50   21490939.125 ±  114301.740  ops/s
SSZTypes.BitlistBenchmark.getAttestingIndicies  thrpt   50    5192560.185 ±   38629.721  ops/s
SSZTypes.BitlistBenchmark.intersects            thrpt   50   24193985.018 ±  122543.575  ops/s
SSZTypes.BitlistBenchmark.setAllBits            thrpt   50   14888628.761 ±   68087.381  ops/s

New implementation:
Benchmark                                        Mode  Cnt          Score         Error  Units
SSZTypes.BitlistBenchmark.countSetBits          thrpt   50  248619832.534 ±  798031.959  ops/s
SSZTypes.BitlistBenchmark.getAttestingIndicies  thrpt   50    8242911.743 ±   44240.344  ops/s
SSZTypes.BitlistBenchmark.intersects            thrpt   50  332067959.309 ± 1628059.852  ops/s
SSZTypes.BitlistBenchmark.setAllBits            thrpt   50   37762009.852 ± 1689423.217  ops/s
```

title: Aggregate and include all available attestations in blocks
body:
## PR Description
Replace `BlockAttestationPool` which only stored aggregates with `AggregatingAttestationPool`.  All attestations are tracked in this pool and are aggregated on demand when producing blocks or when a validator is assigned as the aggregator for a committee.

The aggregation approach is semi-intelligent.  Currently it uses an arbitrary order for selecting one of the available `AttestationData`. For a single `AttestationData` it will create the aggregate by attempting to include attestations in order of the number of validators they include.  This has a reasonable chance of fitting the most validators into each aggregate while minimising the amount we have to aggregate.

In future work, when creating blocks we should create an aggregate based on the `AttestationData` which has the greatest number of unique validators attesting for it first.

title: Add SyncStatusTracker to consider multiple variables when deciding if the node is in sync
body:
## PR Description
Introduces `SyncStatusTracker` to provide a more nuanced algorithm to determine if the node is in sync than just checking if the sync service is running a sync.

When the node first starts up, it is in `START_UP` state.  It moves out of `START_UP` state when either a minimum number of peers are connected, a timeout is reached or syncing begins.  After that point if a sync is running the state is `SYNCING`, otherwise it's `IN_SYNC`.

`ValidatorApiHandler` only calculates duties once the node is `IN_SYNC` avoiding the problem of trying to process huge numbers of blocks at startup because the request for duties came in before any peers were connected.

`SyncStatusTracker` is specifically designed so that in the future it can emit events indicating when the state changes (making it a push model, not just pull).

The minimum number of peers and timeout on startup need to be made configurable and tuned. The defaults should vary depending on the network being connected to (specifically minimal should skip START_UP as it's likely to be a single instance).

body:
## PR Description
Previously, if loading validator duties failed because the node was syncing, it was not retried, so up to two epochs had to pass before validators would begin performing their duties. 
Additionally, when errors that could be retried occurred repeatedly the validator client would never give up requesting duties for that epoch. Now once the epoch has passed, retries are aborted.

Also fixes the `--X` CLI args for startup conditions to have a double `-` prefix instead of single.

title: Improve genesis performance and logging
body:
## PR Description
Improve the user experience around startup.

1. Send status logs to the console which logging mode is set to "both". They're important messages that shouldn't be hidden off in the log file.
2. Provide status logs indicating which mode of genesis is being used (load from existing store on disk, load from genesis file, mock genesis or eth1 chain).
3. Count the number of activated validators in `GenesisGenerator` instead of having to generate the state and iterate through all validators counting them.
4. Send requests for ETH1 block data in increasing order of block number so that the data we get back first can be immediately sent off for processing. Previously we sent requests in reverse order and so wound up waiting for them all to complete before processing any deposits
5. Add status logs to report when min genesis time is reached and for each full percentage of required validators added so the user can see progress towards genesis.
6. Reduce log level for invalid deposits to debug instead of warn. They're really very common and probably not yours so you don't care.

- Extract block verification into a separate class
- Optimize BLS signatures verification by batching them: https://ethresear.ch/t/fast-verification-of-multiple-bls-signatures/5407
- Optimize batch BLS with parallelization
- Optimize batch BLS with doing `ate2` instead of `ate` (not very big gain and only for large batches)

title: Add options to connect to a chain with ETH1 disabled
body:
## PR Description
Make the `--Xinterop-start-state` a "real" option `--initial-state` to allow starting the chain from an initial state from a file or URL.
Add `--eth1-enabled` option (defaults to true) to allow disabling loading of data from the ETH1 chain.

This enables a variety of scenarios:
 * Syncing a beacon node to an existing network without running validators (`--eth1-enabled=false --initial-state=<genesis.ssz>` (eth1 data is only required to find genesis and create new blocks so unneeded in this case)
 * Allowing a beacon node to start syncing blocks before it has caught up with ETH1 deposits (`--initial-state=<genesis.ssz>`.  Avoids the delay in determining genesis from the ETH1 chain before existing blocks can start to be downloaded an imported.

If ETH1 is disabled and no initial state is provided, Teku can still start from an existing database which would provide the initial state to work from.  If there is also no initial state in the database, it terminates with an error:
`ETH1 is disabled but initial state is unknown. Enable ETH1 or specify an initial state.`

title: Validate that the attestation bitlist size matches the committee size
body:
## PR Description
When creating an indexed attestation we need to ensure that the aggregation bits are the same size as the committee.  There are four places this can occur:

 * When a `BeaconState` contains invalid `PendingAttestation` waiting processing at the end of the epoch. This will never occur "naturally" but could occur if an invalid start state is provided.
 * When an attestation is received via gossip. We need to create the indexed attestation as part of validating it.
 * As part of running fork choice rule on received attestations. Partial validation was in place here - if the bitlist was too short the attestation was rejected, but if it was too large it was processed.
 * When an attestation is received as part of a block.  Validation is already in place here.

An explicit precondition check has been added in `get_attesting_indices` so that it's now impossible to create an indexed attestation if the bitlist size is incorrect.  All of the above cases now will reject the attestation.  

The gossip attestation validator also performs an explicit check so it can return a standard INVALID result instead of throwing an `IllegalStateException`.  Fork choice now catches `InvalidArgumentException` when creating the indexed attestation instead of `IndexOutOfBoundsException` (which is what was thrown if the bitlist was too short). The other cases already expect and handle the precondition check exception.

## Fixed Issue(s)
fixes #1685 
covers at least part of #1686

title: Fix fork choice race condition
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/artemis/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
Fixes the fork choice race condition described here: [Jira BC-403](https://pegasys1.atlassian.net/browse/BC-403).

#### Analysis of the bug:
- On block occurs, `onBlock` (store) transaction starts
- During `onBlock`, `protoArrayForkChoice` gets updated with block information
- Before `onBlock` transaction finishes committing, and thus saving the block to store, `processHead` starts.
- Since we did not wait for the `onBlock` transaction to finish, in `processHead` when we get the block and call .`getSlot()`, we get a `NPE`. 

#### Fix:
After offline discussion with @mbaxter, we decided that the best way going forward is to make sure `Store` and `ForkChoiceStrategy` are in sync with respect to the elements they reference. So, this PR moves on block transaction creation and commit to the `ForkChoice.onBlock()` method so that `ForkChoiceStategy.onBlock()` only gets called after the `Store` transaction commit is successfully done.
author: cemozerr

title: [BC-415] Rework status message handling
body:
## PR Description
Make sure we return a consistent, valid status message.  

Previously, we were pulling the headRoot and headSlot in separate requests, which could lead to inconsistent head information.  Additionally, if the best block / chainhead was unavailable we would return zero for the headRoot / headSlot.  

This PR makes sure we're returning consistent head information, and reworks our approach to missing chainhead information.  We will now respond with an error if peers try to request status information before we're ready.  Because the network only spins up after this data is available, we shouldn't actually encounter these errors in practice.

title: [BC-415] Rework CombinedChainDataClient.getStateAtSlot()

Also, added some test utilities to make it easier to write integration tests:  
- Added `MockRocksDbInstance`, which allows us to create an in-memory version of `RocksDbDatabase`
- Added `InMemoryStorageSystem` which sets up and wires together an in-memory database with a `RecentChainData` instance, and makes the `RecentChainData` instance as well as a `CombinedChainData` instance available.
- Added a `ChainUpdater` that generates chain data with `ChainGenerator` and immediately adds the data to a `RecentChainData` instance.  

Fixes https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/issues/1713

title: Calculate ETH1 deposit count and root based on event logs
body:
## PR Description
Reworks how `Eth1Data` is collected so that there is no longer a dependency on having ETH1 world state available. All information is built up from the deposit event logs.

On both the PoWService and BeaconChainService sides, `Eth1Data` is now controlled by the deposit handling, rather than separate. This allows us to guarantee that all deposit data is processed before the `Eth1Data` for any empty blocks is filled in.

On the PoWService side:
 1. empty blocks are completely ignored until all deposits are processed up to the ETH1 follow distance from head.  This avoids querying old block data unnecessarily.
 2. Once follow distance has been reached, block data is fetched walking backwards from that latest block until a block is reached with a timestamp prior to the caching period. This handles filling the cache at initial startup
 3. As the chain moves forward, deposits are requested and processed for the unprocessed range, then any blocks without deposits in that range are requested.

On the BeaconChain side:
 * `DepositProvider` continues to receive and process all deposits. After all deposits in a block are processed it notifies `Eth1DataCache` of the block and the new `Eth1Data` associated with that block (generated from the deposit Merkle tree).
 * `DepositProvider` also passes block information for blocks without deposits to `Eth1DataCache`.  `Eth1DataCache` uses the same deposit root and count as the prior block from its cache for this blocks (as with no deposits in the block they must be unchanged).

## Fixed Issue(s)
fixes #1813 
fixes #1863

title: Fix snappy blocking
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description

In the Eth2 RPC code replace blocking handling (aka `InputStream`) with non-blocking `ByteBuf` processing. 

What was done: 
- Adopted Netty Snappy framed Encoder/Decoder for standalone work 
- Replaced all `InputStream`'s with `ByteBuf`'s in RPC code 
- Adopted and extended tests for `ByteBuf`

Benefits: 
- No thread growth for serving `InputStream.read()` waiting for the next response chunk from the wire
- No accident thread leaks in some boundary cases 
- Less bytes copying 

Drawbacks: 
- Too complex and error prone to work with `ByteBuf`s manually since you need to take care of message fragmentation, sticking and `ByteBuf` reference counting 
- Too low-level code in a high-level module 

## TODO
- [x] Test for `ByteBuf` leaks
- [x] Seems like checksum incompatibility between Xerial and Netty compressors
- [x] Respect length limits

title: [#1976] Move hot state management into store
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
As a preliminary step in addressing #1976, move hot state management into the `Store`.  This consolidates hot state management in one place:  previously hot states were kept in both the `Database` and the `Store`.  This change also necessitated moving pruning logic from the `Database` into the `Store`.

Additionally, all knowably non-canonical blocks are now pruned whenever we finalized a new checkpoint.  This includes blocks that do not descend from the latest finalized block and blocks that descend from the latest finalized block, but are at or prior to latest finalized epoch boundary.   For example, if block 30 finalizes epoch 1 (with epoch boundary at slot 32), other blocks at slots 30, 31, or 32 will be pruned as invalid. 

As a result of these changes, a fair number of tests needed to be updated to operate on valid chain data.

title: Reduce memory footprint for hot-state BeaconState instances
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description

Though `BeaconState` is backed up with a remerkable tree, accessing it and reconstructing corresponding `views` (aka vectors, containers, etc.) is a bit expensive from the performance standpoint. That's why these `views` are cached and returned unless their backing subtree is modified. 

However this comes at a cost of the memory footprint. When there are a lot of hot-state `BeaconState` instances resides in memory every instance is keeping the full set of views. This is suboptimal since the `BeaconState`s older than the `head` are most likely wouldn't be accessed or accessed very limited (just a small subset of structures). 

With this PR on any beacon state modification (`BeaconState-1` => `MutableBeaconState` => `BeaconState-2`) when the view caches are `transfer()`ed from `BeaconState-1` to `BeaconState-2` the original caches in the `BeaconState-1` would be cleared. 

This would reduce the memory footprint (in Mb below) of the `BeaconState` instances if they are all kept in memory: 
| Number of states | Before | After |
|------------------|--------|-------|
| 1                | 69     | 69    |
| 32               | 163    | 153   |
| 65               | 187    | 161   |
| 130              | 229    | 172   |
| 390              | 414    | 226   |

** these are consecutive slot states. For sparse states (e.g. on each epoch) the numbers would differ

Some more details here: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1IA8Yq6CgCWfOBy8dTpY-uFVUDYBWCRTSl_-7LoXTA9M/edit?usp=sharing

This doesn't affect performance (at least from the point of `TransitionBenchmark`)

title: Add test case for infinite pubkey and signature
body:
This adds a test to confirm behaviour in the case that a message has both public key and signature being the identity - the points at infinity in their respective subgroups.

It's prompted by [this deposit](https://goerli.etherscan.io/tx/0xa2784acaf5fdcf8cb1e9fe4d416d84a23aa5ff37677846f2a4bf1ce7f9bb1dd4) on Witti which has infinite public key and signature.

I can't find anything in the [IETF draft](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-irtf-cfrg-bls-signature-02) that covers this case, and the math checks out, so I'm assuming this makes sense. There doesn't seem to have been a fork on Witti, and the validator has been inducted, so it looks like Teku, LH and Prysm all agree about this.

title: Start services sequentially so we don't miss ETH1 events
body:
## PR Description
Start services sequentially instead of in parallel to avoid missing ETH1 events.

Generating the genesis state for the Onyx network regularly missed the minimum genesis time event from the PoWService because it occurred before `GenesisHandler` had been setup by the beacon node.

Now we start services in a fixed order - storage, beacon chain, validator client, timer, pow service.  Thus we'll never miss ETH1 events and the storage will be ready to respond to the first request beacon chain makes when requesting data.  Leaving the retry capability in place for now as this may not be the best long term solution but it's a quick way to avoid these kinds of intermittent issues.

title: Move fork choice processing into Store
body:
## PR Description
Move fork choice processing into `Store`, allowing us to:
* Consolidate state processing.  Previously, `Store` would process every state after finalization while initializing, and afterwards we would set up `ProtoArrayForkChoiceStrategy`, which would also process every non-finalized state.  Because `ProtoArrayForkChoiceStrategy` iterated over blocks in a random order, during long periods of non-finalization we could end up reprocessing states many times as we initialized fork choice.  We now initialize `Store` and fork-choice at the same time, walking through non-finalized states only once.
* Avoid manually invoking fork-choice processing in tests whenever blocks are added to the `Store`.  Because fork-choice processing was already partially integrated with `RecentChainData` (we would prune`ProtoArrayForkChoiceStrategy` whenever the latest finalized checkpoint was updated), we previously needed to manually run fork-choice processing on all blocks added to the `Store` in order to avoid errors where we would try to prune `ProtoArrayForkChoiceStrategy` given a block that hadn't yet been processed.
* Lay some groundwork for persisting fork-choice state to disk: having `ProtoArrayForkChoiceStrategy` owned by `Store` should make it easier to persist fork-choice state and keep this state in sync with the rest of our chain data.

## Documentation

title: [Issue 2037] Limit hot blocks kept in memory
body:
## PR Description
Limit hot blocks kept in memory. 

Changes include:
* Pass a `BlockProvider` into `Store`, allowing `Store` to drop blocks from memory, and re-pull them from storage as-needed.  
* Update `StateGenerator` to run with a `BlockProvider` so that it can regenerate states even if the required blocks are not immediately available.
* Update `Database.getStore()` to return a `StoreBuilder` so that the `BlockProvider` (which will call back to the database to retrieve missing blocks) can be set externally.  
* Keep a `HashTree` instance in `Store`, so that even if blocks are dropped, we can calculate which blocks are known, what hashes have been finalized, and what blocks are required to regenerate states

Remaining TODO's:
* The `Store` retrieves blocks asynchronously by calling to storage, but all API's are still synchronous.  We need to rework the API's to use futures where necessary.

title: Fix fork choice update head race condition
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
Fixes the race condition that resulted in `java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: ProtoArray: Invalid delta length`

`Store.updateHead` method, which updates our head block using our `ForkChoiceStrategy` and manipulates internal Store variables when doing so, previously did not have any read or write locks as it accessed and manipulated the Store state. Since this method reads and adds writes to be committed during the `commit` method of the Transaction, it has to make sure that it doesn't read a state that might be now redundant. For that, it needs to obtain a read lock.

title: Optimize memory:  keep BeaconState view caches via SoftReference
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description

Keep the roots of remerkable view caches (`BeaconStateImpl`) via `SoftReference` so in case of heap memory lack they can be released. 

The fix doesn't affect performance as only the topmost views (`BeaconState` children views) are accessed by `SoftReference` 

This is not ideal solution, since arbitrary caches are erased instead of 'last recently used'. 
But the latter approach would be more complex and error-prone. While the current solution is pretty simple, reliable and allows to avoid OOM at the expense of possible ~2x `BeaconState` structures access slowdown

title: tweak write buffer down to 128MB after some extra testing
body:
When testing with 256MB write buffer, we get into a weird situation where the write buffer uses over 1GB of disk, then goes back down. Seen around slot 34000 on witti syncing.

When i reduced the write buffer to 128MB, the disk usage doesn't seem to spike like that, it goes a little way forward then goes back to a better level. It also doesn't have a whole stack of flushes, though there's a couple a minute. This should be a good starting point, but it may need to be a user settable feature in the future.

The archive database definitely doesn't need a large write buffer, so we should also consider reducing that to around 16MB by default, but that was not done in this PR.

title: [Issue 2037] Limit hot blocks in memory (with race condition fix)
body:
## PR Description
Limit hot blocks kept in memory.  

This PR reapplies reverted changes from  #2211 with an additional fix for a race condition. The following example scenario illustrates the race condition: 
* Transaction A adds a block.
* Transaction A is committed and we [pre-calculate changes](https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/blob/5380e888871def02e4541c0f2ca8cba1f37d2c8d/storage/src/main/java/tech/pegasys/teku/storage/store/Store.java#L516) to be applied.
  * These changes included a new `blockTree` containing the newly added block.
* Then, transaction B starts (updating something irrelevant to the chain data like `time`).
* Transaction B commits, and pre-calculates its changes. 
  * These pre-calculations are based on the existing data in `Store` which does not contain the pending changes from Transaction A.  So, the updated `blockTree` calculated here does not contain the new block from Transaction A.
* Transaction A [finishes committing](https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/blob/5380e888871def02e4541c0f2ca8cba1f37d2c8d/storage/src/main/java/tech/pegasys/teku/storage/store/Store.java#L529), applying the new `blockTree` with its new block.
* Transaction B finishes committing, overwriting the `blockTree` with its version which is missing the new block from Transaction A.  Now, the new block is no longer tracked.

The fix is to only calculate and apply `blockTree` updates when the tree is actually modified (new blocks are added or a new finalized root is set).  Because all block updates are `synchronized`, we won't encounter this race condition.  

## Fixed Issue(s)
Fixes #2037

title: Report unknown block instead of throwing NullPointerException
body:
## PR Description
It's possible that the block targeted by an attestation is dropped from the store while we're processing the attestation. We could wind up passing the initial check that the block is known because it hasn't been pruned from protoarray when we do that check and then later fail to create the checkpoint state for that target because the block isn't available in the store resulting in a `NullPointerException`.

If the checkpoint state is unavailable, the target block must be unknown so defer the attestation. Worst case the block is invalid and the attestation gets dropped once it is too old.

To reduce the risk of this in future, `getCheckpointState` now returns an `Optional`.

title: Prioritise based on attestation subnets when connecting and disconnecting peers
body:
## PR Description
To be able to publish attestations, Teku needs to ensure it has at least one peer connected that is subscribed to each attestation subnet.  To help do that when connecting to or disconnecting from peer, we rank the peers based on the subnets they are subscribed to and how many other peers we have already subscribed to that subnet.

When connecting, we only have the persistent subnets advertised in the peer's ENR to base the decision off but once connected we use the peer's actual subscriptions, which includes persistent and short term subscriptions. This ensures that the subscriptions we score a peer on are always up to date even if we don't have their latest ENR and avoids issues with peers advertising a lot of subnets in their ENR but not actually subscribing to them.

The scoring system is designed to give high scores to peers that subscribe to subnets with no or few subscribers and very quickly reduce the score boost for subnets that have more peers. It's a pretty arbitrary algorithm but seems to give reasonable results and is definitely better than randomly picking peers.

To fully ensure we have all subnets covered, we should also continue attempting to connect to peers even if we have reached our peer limit if there are subnets with limited subscribers and discovered peers claim to subscribe to those subnets.  Potentially we could also retry sending attestations for a short period if we don't have a peer to send them to when first produced. Those changes are for follow up PRs.

## Fixed Issue(s)
Part of #1963

title: Fix rpc handler close future leak
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description

- Avoid leaking references to the Libp2p `Connection.closeFuture`. (details below) 
- Make `RpcHandler.sendRequest()` code a bit cleaner with using new `SafeFuture.orInterrupt()` feature 

`Connection.closeFuture` may be very long living future in terms it may keep uncompleted for very long time (while we are connected to a peer). Meanwhile there are many streams (and their handlers) are created which derive from this future this or that way to be aware of the parent channel close while setting up a child Stream. 

The problem is when you are deriving any other future from the `Connection.closeFuture` (in any ways like `thenApply`, `whenComplete` etc) that future would remain referenced together with all closures refs until the `Connection.closeFuture` is complete (which may never happen). 

There are no means for `CompletableFuture` to remove this dependency later (unlike `netty.Future.add/removeListener`). The only mean the dependency can be removed is via `CompletableFuture.anyOf` (or `.*either*`) methods, so when the 'main' future is completed all other futures are released. 

This way I implemented `SafeFuture.orInterrupt()` concept. 
- it doesn't accumulate dependent future refs inside interruption futures (like `closeFuture`)
- it prevents further async tasks from being executed when interruption occurs (when inserted together with every async task)
- seems like it can make that async hell a bit cleaner 

## Fixed Issue(s)
Relates #2286 (though most likely the Libp2p fix is the primary for resolving this issue https://github.com/libp2p/jvm-libp2p/commit/7030249a80e944b7f463d68e54a1b892e148a60b)

title: Ensure validator indices in attester slashings are valid
body:
## PR Description
`AttestaterSlashing` objects include an `IndexedAttestation` opening up the possibility that the validator indices it specifies are out of bounds for the validator list. Normally this isn't an issue because we index the attestation ourselves so know the indices are valid. 

`SignedAggregateAndProof` also includes a validator index which must be verified to be in range before looking up the validator public key.

To ensure this category of errors is avoided, `ValidatorsUtil.getValidatorPubKey` now performs bounds checking and returns an empty `Optional` if the index is out of range.  Callers are updated to handle this and fail validation of the public key is not available.

## Fixed Issue(s)

title: Maintain a minimum number of randomly selected peers
body:
## PR Description
Rather than selecting all peers based on their score, maintain a minimum number of randomly selected peers. This has two key benefits:
1. provides sybil resistance as randomly selected peers must be ones we've selected, and which are not affected by the scoring system
2. improves connectivity for nodes which are not running validators and so aren't subscribed to any subnets. Previously these would also be the first peers to be dropped but now at least have a chance of being randomly selected and preserved.

title: Deliver EventChannel responses on a publisher owned thread
body:
## PR Description
When an `EventChannel` returns a future, previously it was completed on the channel's subscriber thread, which meant that any chained actions also happened on the subscriber thread and had to complete before the subscriber could move on to the next event.

Instead, for any `EventChannel` that can return a future, creating a publisher now requires specifying an `AsyncRunner` which is used to complete the returned future.  This way the chained actions are all completed on a thread owned by the publisher's service, not the subscribers.  As a specific example, when the validator service makes a call to `ValidatorApiChannel`, the call is handled in the beacon chain on a thread dedicated to `ValidatorApiChannel`, but the returned future is completed by the `AsyncRunner` the validator service provided when creating its publisher.  So execution correctly moves from validator service to beacon service and then back.

If the channel doesn't return values (all methods return `void`), a publisher can be created without specifying an `AsyncRunner`, otherwise one is required.  This is achieved by introducing two marker interfaces - `ChannelInterface` and `NonReturningChannelInterface` which extends it.  All event channels must extend one of those and that's enforced by the compiler.  A runtime check is performed to reject creating an `EventChannel` for an interface that extends `NonReturningEventChannel` if it has any methods that return something other than `void`.

The additional benefit of the marker interfaces is that it's simple to find all interfaces which are used with event channels which was slightly challenging previously.

## Fixed Issue(s)
fixes #2347

title: Report errors that occur when executing a task on the worker thread pool
body:
##  PR Description

When `ScheduledExecutorAsyncRunner` run a delayed task, if when the task became due, the worker thread pool rejected it the error would be silently ignored. This resulted in tasks executed via `runWithFixedDelay` no longer repeating as the last execution never completed.

Now the rejection exception is reported back to the caller so it will be handled correctly and repeating tasks will continue repeating.  #2362 includes a fix to make it dramatically less likely that tasks will be rejected.

## Fixed Issue(s)
Fixes at least one part of #2200 because the `ConnectionManager` uses `runWithFixedDelay` and when it stops executing Teku stops making new connections to peers.

title: [Refactor] Extract factory to create thread pools
body:
## PR Description
Given the difficulties getting a thread pool to work the way we need, extract a factory to create them with predictable behaviour and automatically track useful metrics.

Adds a test to confirm the thread pool behaviour is as we expect.

The `metrics` module no longer depends on `util` which makes it possible for things in `util` or other modules that `util` uses to use metrics. The one key piece of this is that it can no longer use `TekuConfiguration` so exposes a `MetricsConfig` interface which `TekuConfiguration` implements.  Happy to have push back on this if others disagree but it feels like a reasonable way forward to gradually split up `TekuConfiguration` instead of having one giant config object for everything.

Having `metrics` not depend on `utils` allows `ScheduledExecutorAsyncRunner` to be moved to the `async` package rather than having to be in service utils and the new `MetricsTrackingExecutorFactory` can be extracted out to the `async` package as well rather than also having to be in service utils.

title: Don't mark peers as permanently unsuitable when they fail to respond to ping
body:
## PR Description
When the network connection is interrupted in a way that the local machine can't immediately detect (e.g. router suddenly powering off) all connected peers wind up being disconnected because they don't respond to pings.  Previously this caused them to be marked as permanently unsuitable and Teku would no longer initiate connections to them (incoming connections would still be accepted).

Now not responding to pings invokes a temporary penalty but after that Teku will again initiate connections to the peer.  On small networks this significantly improves the ability to recover after a network outage.

## Fixed Issue(s)
fixes #2200

title: Handle peers limiting request block by range responses
body:
## PR Description
Handle peers responding with only some of the blocks in the requested range.  If the peer excessively throttles the responses (for example only returning one block) then we fail the sync against that peer.  The `SyncManager` will avoid selecting that peer as a sync target for a period and select a different target peer.  We don't disconnect the peer.

If the peer's response allows us to progress at least 50 slots in our sync, we consider it reasonable throttling and continue using the peer as our sync target.

It is possible for a peer to hit this condition when they aren't throttling excessively if there are a lot of empty blocks. e.g if we request block 1-200 and the only block in that range is at slot 2, we will assume the peer is throttling excessively.  The next peer we selected would then return no blocks and we'd then know that all blocks were empty and move on.

## Fixed Issue(s)
fixes #1957

## PR Description

This PR introduces a new service in Teku, the Remote Validator service. This service allows remote validators to connect to the beacon node and receive events.

Important parts:
- `RemoteValidatorService`: the actual service class that coordinates the wiring of all components together
- `RemoteValidatorSubscriptions`: the class that maintains the active subscriptions and broadcast events to subscribers
- `RemoteValidatorApi`: the WebSocket service that is used as a channel to publish the messages
- `RemoteValidatorBeaconChainEventsAdapter`: this class listens to all events that a subscriber is interested in.

title: Increase read timeout for ETH1 requests
body:
## PR Description
Increases the read timeout for ETH1 requests to give ETH1 nodes more time to respond given that we may be requesting a large number of log events.

Limit the maximum number of blocks we'll request deposit events for.  We still wind up with a single big request up to the min genesis time block but this avoids having a continually growing number of deposits to parse in a single request. Previously we would request 0 -> min-genesis and then min-genesis -> HEAD - after the chain has run for a number of years the min-genesis -> HEAD request might have millions of deposit events.  With the new limit in place we request 0 -> min-genesis in one go but then at most 500,000 blocks at a time so the result size doesn't grow completely unbounded.

title: [Issue 2334] Fix state transition committee cache
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
This PR fixes an issue where our state transition caches were being corrupted with invalid committee data.

I was able to reproduce this corrupted cache issue as follows:
* Start a single node network with 64 validators
* Let the network run for a bit and finalize some epochs
* Stop the node and let several epoch pass
* Restart the node, at which point we would get "Invalid attestation: Signature is invalid" errors

On restart, the node would calculate and schedule upcoming validator duties correctly.  However, when we went to produce our attestations, we would try to calculate committee information using an old state (from the head of the chain) without processing slots forward to the slot being queried.  The calculated committee information from the stale state would then end up being cached by our `TransitionCaches` object.  This caused subsequent queries to pull committee information to return invalid data.  This then caused us to view our produced attestations as invalid because the corrupted committee information was inconsistent with the produced attestation. 

The fix is to ensure that any state used to calculate committee information is in range of the slot being queried (the state must be from at least the previous epoch).  Checks have been added to `CommitteeUtil.get_beacon_committee()` to make sure we don't allow old states to be used for this calculation. `ChainDataProvider` and `ValidatorApiHandler` have been updated to run with states that have been processed up to an appropriate epoch before trying to calculate committee information.

## Fixed Issue(s)
Fixes #2334 
Fixes #2446

title: [Issue 2334] Rework transition cache fix
body:
<!-- Thanks for sending a pull request! Please check out our contribution guidelines: -->
<!-- https://github.com/PegaSysEng/teku/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

## PR Description
This PR reworks the logic from #2501, fixing a bug introduced there with attestation production.

In retrospect, the bug introduced in that PR is pretty obvious 🤦‍♀️. The attestation logic was modified to ensure that the state used to produce our attestation is rolled forward if the latest block at the assigned slot is very old.  When trying to optimize by pulling a checkpoint state from our cache, the attestation production logic was modified to rely exclusively on the checkpoint block and state from the previous epoch.  This doesn't work for normal case where the latest block state doesn't need to be rolled forward - instead of attesting to the latest block, we end up attesting to an out-of-date block from the previous epoch boundary.  

Fixed to only pull the checkpoint state if the latest block is too old.

## Fixed Issue(s)
Fixes #2334
Fixes #2446
